tells: One clear idea: a flat black silhouette of an executive falls through a modernist office and a tower of period advertising, so the title is a metaphor for the show's whole story.
Every frame is built differently: a wide shot of the office from behind, a low close-up on the shoes, a tiny falling figure against a curtain-wall façade, and a big foreground figure tumbling.
Vintage ad imagery (a pin-up, a whisky glass, the line 'Enjoy the best America has to offer') sits translucently on the window grid, giving dense, meaningful layers.
Credits are set in a period grotesque with the first name in red caps and the surname in black. The system is restrained and confident, and the credits sit as part of the composition.
The ending reverses the fall into a calm pose on the sofa, holding a cigarette. That is a real narrative payoff with surprise and wit.
A deliberate palette of warm grey ground, flat black, red accent and desaturated ad colour, plus a paper-grain texture.
gaps: The interior in the opening frame is a little flat and diagrammatic next to the richness of the ad montage.
The light is mostly graphic rather than physical. A touch more atmospheric depth in the office space would add weight.
With such a small credit type, some credits get lost over the busier montage frames.

tells: A specific concept: the world is shown as a clockwork map whose cities grow mechanically from the board, and an astrolabe sun binds them together. It also works as an orientation device for viewers.
Materials are rich and convincing: engraved metal bands, wood, brass gears, aged parchment, and shallow depth of field that reads like a tabletop miniature.
The light is motivated and dramatic. The armillary sun blows out into warm flares, and the map pieces carry practical-looking shadows.
Choreography varies: macro close-ups of the engraved band, low tracking shots across the cities, gears assembling, a top-down map view, and a symmetrical title lock-up.
The credits use a classical inscriptional serif with a small sigil icon for each credit, which ties into the world's heraldry.
Bronze, slate and parchment make a cohesive, period-appropriate palette.
gaps: The credit typography is set small and low-contrast, so legibility over busy detail suffers in places.
The final title lock-up, with its ornate symmetrical crest and glowing serif, is the most conventional frame in an otherwise inventive piece.
The palette is almost entirely warm, so a cooler counterpoint for the colder northern locations is missing.

tells: The typography is the subject. Latin and katakana letterforms are broken into modular fragments, pixel grids and stencilled geometry, and the piece resolves into 'TOKYO' with Japanese mixed into the letters.
The palette is deliberate and unusual: hot pink, cyan, acid lime and violet on deep aubergine-black, and it changes from shot to shot.

Each frame uses a different structure: a giant cropped letter, a horizontal scan band, a framed letter field, diagonal rotated type, an LED dot matrix, and a dense layered collage. That is real choreography, not a repeated layout.
Print and scanline texture plus grain give the digital material some tactility.
The density and layering are controlled, and the scale contrast is strong.
gaps: There is no emotional or narrative arc to match A or B. It is a highly accomplished typographic exercise rather than an idea about a place.
The glitch-and-dot-matrix vocabulary is a familiar 'Tokyo cyber' aesthetic and risks cliché, so it needs a more personal visual language.
The light is purely graphic, with no real depth or physical light, so the frames can feel uniformly flat across the sequence.

Some of the transparent ad layering reads as simple opacity stacking. More intentional compositing (masking, halftone) would deepen the falling frames.
The credit type is small and placed conventionally in the lower third mid-fall. It could interact with the architecture more.

gaps: The title lockup's bevelled, glowing, trajan-esque treatment is more conventional than the rest of the piece.
In the map frames the credit type sits low-contrast against busy terrain, so legibility suffers in places.
The heavy bloom and vignette sometimes flatten the midtones and slightly obscure the craft of the miniatures.

tells: The typography is the subject. Latin letterforms are broken into modular glyphs, mixed with katakana fragments and dot-matrix pixel letters, and the 'TOKYO' wordmark is assembled from components.
The palette is deliberate and unusual: hot pink, cyan, acid lime, violet and yellow on near-black, signal colours that suit Tokyo's signage.

There is real variety between frames: a giant cropped 'D' and target, a horizontal band, a lime frame of scattered glyphs, a diagonal axis, an LED grid, and a collaged finale. This is not one layout with the words swapped.
Subtle print and grain texture plus layered UI-like fragments make the frames dense rather than empty.
Scale contrast is strong: full-bleed letters against tiny tracked glyphs.
gaps: The idea is a style (Tokyo as glitchy signage typography) rather than a narrative or a single memorable mechanism like B's clockwork map.
There is no light or depth. Everything is flat graphic, so it lacks B's material richness and its sense of a physical world.
The glitch and datamosh vocabulary is well worn. It needs one surprising move that only this piece could make to stand out at award level.

tells: The specific idea: a silhouetted ad man walks into his office, the office dissolves, and he falls past skyscrapers papered with period advertising, then lands in the iconic sofa pose. It is a Saul Bass echo turned into character and theme.
Every frame works as a poster: black flat silhouettes against desaturated, half-tone vintage ad photography projected onto glass façades.
The palette is disciplined, black, bone and one red accent, and the red is used only for names, which ties the type to the system.
The typography has a period-correct grotesk with a two-tone red/black split for credits and title, placed to balance each composition.
The choreography is clear and strong: establish, walk, fall, fall closer, then resolve. Scale and angle change dramatically between frames.
Paper grain and screen texture on the ad layers add age and material.
gaps: The light is mostly flat by design, so it has less atmospheric depth than B.
The office establishing frame is sparse and illustrative compared with the dense falling sequences.
Some credit placements over the busy ad imagery lose hierarchy, for example the 'Enjoy the best America has to offer' line competing with the credits.

defects: The move into the end card is a plain cross-dissolve. Frame 4 shows a grey, half-transparent bird ghosting over the sun and sky, which reads as two layers fighting, not a transformation.

The wingbeat is a 2D flip of the wing shapes about a fixed pivot. The body never bobs, the tail never fans to correct, and the primaries never bend, so there is no lift or weight. A hovering kestrel is defined by its still head and constantly working body, and that is missing.
The pairs show only small differences in wing angle. The cycle looks uniform and possibly linear, with no hold at the top or snap on the downstroke.
The grass, clouds and sun are effectively static (per-second change is about 8). The background is a still plate with no wind, even though the soundtrack carries a wind bed.
The end card is static for about 2 s, from 3.8 s to 6.0 s: the wordmark and bird simply sit there, with no settle, light move or breath.
The KESTREL wordmark is a generic wide-tracked serif placed under the mark. It fades in with no relation to the hover or the flight.
The grass is uniform procedural spikes with near-identical tapers and a hard horizon band. The texture repeats across the width.

Audio: the noise bed is a perfect rectangle in the spectrogram (1.2–3.76 s). It starts and stops abruptly, is band-limited flat to about 20 kHz, and has no envelope or movement, so it reads as generated white noise, not a recorded or designed wind.
Audio: the low drone is static harmonic stacking for the full length, with no musical event or hit on the logo reveal beyond the noise cutting out.
gaps: Motion: there is no hover physics or choreography. Top studios would animate the kestrel's signature (the locked head, the working wings and tail, and the gust-and-correct rhythm) and build tension to a stoop or a wing-snap that drives the reveal. Instead the piece holds one repeated flap and then dissolves.

Transition and arc: the strongest idea (the sunset carried inside the silhouette) arrives through a soft crossfade. It should be a designed, motivated move, such as the sun eclipsing behind the body, a light wipe or a match-cut on the wing apex, landing on a peak and then settling with overshoot.

Sound: the soundtrack is a static drone plus a hard-gated block of white noise. It needs real design: shaped wind with movement, wing-beat foley synced to each downstroke, a tonal swell into the reveal and a resolved logo sting with a tail.
